title: Day 784: Mexico Deploys 3,400 More Troops and Agents to Sinaloa After US Citizen's Killing
detail: On Tuesday, September 15, 2026, Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch announced an additional 3,400 federal military and security personnel for Sinaloa, a day after a US citizen was shot dead in Mazatlán and the port recorded four homicides in a single day. The surge is composed of 1,600 Army troops (including 100 special forces, flown to Mazatlán aboard a Boeing 727) plus 1,000 Navy (Semar) elements and 836 additional SSPC federal agents (following 300 SSPC agents and 50 patrol units already sent to Mazatlán on September 13). García Harfuch said the deployment 'strengthens territorial presence, patrols, surveillance, prevention and deterrence,' with focus on Mazatlán, Culiacán and the state's main highways. The reinforcement brings federal personnel in Sinaloa to roughly 20,000, on top of more than 15,900 Defense Ministry elements already operating in the state. Officials cited 2026 year-to-date results of 1,026 detained, 2,031 firearms seized and 47.9 tonnes of drugs confiscated, alongside a claimed 26.1% year-over-year drop in the average daily homicide rate.

title: Day 784: Culiacán Holds First Public Grito de Independencia in Two Years, Governor Domínguez Calls for Peace
detail: On the night of September 15, 2026, Culiacán and other Sinaloa municipalities held public Independence Day 'Grito' ceremonies for the first time since 2024, when the massive events were suspended because of the Chapitos–Mayiza war. Before more than 20,000 people at the Palacio de Gobierno esplanade, interim Governor Graciela Domínguez Nava — Sinaloa's first woman to lead the ceremony — received the national flag from an escort of the 94th Infantry Battalion at 10:20 PM, rang the balcony bell and gave the traditional 'vivas' to Independence heroes, closing with 'Viva el amor al prójimo! Viva la paz!' Mazatlán held its own celebration under reinforced security (roughly 300 state elements and 50 patrols), while Escuinapa reversed an initial cancellation to hold a scaled-back, strictly ceremonial version after recent killings and violence against women in the municipality. Federal officials said the cartel remains diminished but retains meaningful firepower and economic capacity.

media.caption: Governor Graciela Domínguez Nava leads Culiacán's first public Grito de Independencia in two years, September 15, 2026
